defaults.permitted_development: A true self-contained annexe in England should not be assumed to be permitted development and will often need planning permission. Some ancillary family accommodation can be achieved through normal extension rules or a detached Class E building, but the use must stay genuinely subordinate to the main house rather than becoming a second dwelling.

rules.height_rules: Where a detached ancillary building relies on Class E, keep it single storey with eaves up to 2.5m, up to 4m overall for a dual-pitched roof, up to 3m for any other roof and no more than 2.5m overall within 2m of a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate annexe depth allowance. Attached accommodation has to fit within the normal extension rules, while detached space has to stay within the curtilage and 50% coverage limits and still read as ancillary rather than a second home.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary siting matters both for the Class E height cap and for whether the building still reads as subordinate. On designated land, side locations can lose permitted development rights, and listed-building curtilages need full planning permission for outbuildings.
rules.roof_rules: If the proposal relies on Class E, keep the detached building single storey and visually subordinate. Roof terraces, balconies and overtly house-like upper-storey forms usually move annexe proposals outside the ordinary householder route.
rules.materials_rules: If annexe accommodation is allowed, materials, servicing, entrances and internal facilities should reinforce the link with the main dwelling rather than suggest a freestanding new house. A fully independent layout is far more likely to need permission.

rules.permitted_development: A true annexe should not be assumed to be permitted development. Ordinary householder rights can cover an extension or detached building only while the space remains ancillary to the main house; once it operates as self-contained living accommodation, a planning application is usually needed.

rules.height_rules: If a detached building is being relied on as incidental development, the usual outbuilding height limits apply: single storey only, eaves up to 2.5m, up to 4m overall with a dual-pitched roof or 3m for other roof forms, reducing to 2.5m overall within 2m of a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate annexe depth allowance. Attached accommodation has to fit the normal extension rules, while detached space has to stay within the curtilage and 50% coverage limits and still read as ancillary rather than a second home.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary siting matters for both physical bulk and independence of use. A detached building set hard against a boundary, with its own facilities and access, is more likely to be treated as a separate planning unit rather than an incidental outbuilding.
rules.roof_rules: If the proposal relies on outbuilding rights, keep it single storey and visually subordinate. Roof terraces, house-like upper floors and dominant two-storey forms usually move the project away from ordinary householder permitted development.
rules.materials_rules: Annexe accommodation that needs permission is often conditioned to remain ancillary to the main dwelling. Materials, servicing, entrances and window layout should make the building read as part of the same residential plot rather than a freestanding new house.

restrictions.conservation_area: Additional planning restrictions may apply in conservation areas.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent is required for works affecting listed buildings.
restrictions.article4_notes: No borough-wide Article 4 note is recorded here, but site-specific directions or planning conditions can still remove permitted development rights on particular properties.

rules.permitted_development: The critical distinction is between ancillary family accommodation and a separate planning unit. If the building or rooms would function as self-contained living accommodation, you should expect a planning application rather than relying on ordinary householder rights.

rules.height_rules: Detached ancillary space can only borrow the ordinary outbuilding height rules while it remains incidental: single storey, eaves no more than 2.5m, 4m overall with a dual-pitched roof, 3m with another roof form and 2.5m overall near a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: Instead of a dedicated annexe projection right, the planning route depends on form and use: extensions follow the normal extension rules, while detached structures must stay within the usual outbuilding limits and remain clearly ancillary.
rules.boundary_rules: Where the annexe-style space sits close to a boundary, the authority will usually look at both scale and independence. Separate access, servicing and a self-contained layout point away from ordinary householder rights.
rules.roof_rules: Roof form matters because it can make the building look like a second dwelling. Single-storey, subordinate forms are the safest option; roof terraces and dominant upper-storey accommodation usually need a fuller planning route.
rules.materials_rules: The external treatment should reinforce that the accommodation belongs to the same dwellinghouse plot. Separate-house cues such as an autonomous front door arrangement, independent servicing and overtly domestic detailing can make the proposal harder to justify.
